newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore refiners face poor margins on high crude.
newsitem.headline: Singapore refiners face poor margins on high crude.

text.p: Soaring diesel prices have failed to lift profit margins for Singapore refiners as a rally in other oil products is lagging a rise in crude prices, industry sources said on Thursday.
Relatively weaker prices for gasoline, naphtha and jet fuel have pushed margins into the red in October, they said.
Basic refining margins in Singapore since late September have hovered between breakeven and 50-cent losses for every barrel of crude refined, a trader at an oil major said.
Singapore refiners, who produce about 1.2 million barrels of products per day, are not planning immediate cuts in production to try to improve margins. But pressure is mounting for cuts, they said.
Weak margins prompted Singapore's refiners to cut production in the third quarter. Only Esso Singapore has maintained its 15 percent cut.
In the face of the current losses, refiners are running more complex units, which re-process cheaper fuels into more lucrative products like diesel, at maximum levels.
Also the refiners are more selective in the type of crude they purchase on a spot basis, preferring those that are easier to process into diesel, like Malaysia's Tapis and Australia's Kutubu.
"The Far East margins got hit because of the strength of western crude and gas oil," one refiner said.
Refineries make their money be selling products they produce for more than the crude they buy. But if crude prices rise more than product prices, refiners lose out.
"For margins to improve, crude prices and gas oil prices in the west need to be corrected as Asian consumers are reluctant to buy products at such high prices," another major said.
While product prices in Asia are lagging their western counterparts, regional and Middle East crude prices have risen in tandem with western crude prices to around five year highs.
Front-month Brent crude futures, a global benchmark, hit a fresh post-Gulf War high on Tuesday of $24.58 per barrel, dragging regional crudes higher.
Asian benchmark Tapis crude was assessed at $25.75 per barrel for November deliveries -- its highest level since hitting more than $39.00 during the 1990/1991 Gulf War.

Dubai and Arab Light crude oil, the most heavily used by Singapore refiners was assessed at post Gulf War highs on Thursday at $22.09 per barrel and $22.62 respectively, both on a free-on-board Gulf basis.

In stark contrast, prices of some products like gasoline and naphtha are up to $5 per barrel below their post Gulf War highs and prices are not expected to rise much as they face a weak demand period of the year.

Jet/kerosene, the product that's most in demand during the winter for heating, is not living up to expectations. Prices have edged down to $29.50 for October cargoes compared with a peak of almost $34.00 per barrel seen in January.
Fuel oil hit a five-year high on Wednesday of $19 per barrel, but relative to crude it is still undervalued, one trader said.
Diesel has kept pace with the high crude price, bubbling at five-year highs of $29.80 per barrel for the past few days.
"Apart from diesel, all the other products are weaker when compared to current crude prices," one major lamented.

Players said demand for products such as jet fuel, diesel and fuel oil are low for this time of the year as the big buyers in India, China and Japan are not willing to build up stocks at such high prices.
